newsitem.title: UK: Britain ponders privatisation of London metro.
newsitem.headline: Britain ponders privatisation of London metro.

text.p: Britain's cash-strapped London Underground railway system could be sold off to the private sector according to leaked government proposals drawn up under a review by deputy prime minister John Prescott.

The proposals include selling a controlling stake in the ageing metro system known as the "Tube", which is desperately in need of a major cash injection to prevent it crumbling into further disrepair.
Prescott's document, which was leaked by the British Broadcasting Corporation's (BBC) Panorama current affairs programme, described the issue as "urgent".
He had told the programme in a recorded interview to be broadcast later on Monday that he acknowledged the problems.
"I'm talking about radical (changes)...and making some fundamental changes to the long term of this industry," Prescott told Panorama.
The move was immediately welcomed by private transport operators.
Chris Moyes, commercial director at Go-Ahead Group Plc which operates rail passenger services in the London area, said his company would be interested in the bidding if the deal was right.

"Rail companies will be interested and perhaps more qualified than other players to run a high frequency, high density service like the tube. We would be interested, subject to the way it is structured," he told Reuters.

According to the BBC, Prescott has drawn up four possible options to revitalise the network. One is privatisation modelled on the lines of the break-up of the former national rail network British Rail.
This would involve splitting the metro into two companies -- one infrastructure company and one operating company.
Another idea would be to have a single company controlling both trains and infrastructure.
In both cases the government would consider allowing a private sector company hold the controlling stake in the metro.
The third option is selling off individual metro rail lines and the last is to allow a franchisee to run the entire network.
After news of the leak, Prescott responded with anger. He said the documents had been "stolen" from his offices by BBC reporters who had "sensationalised" its contents.
However, Prescott concluded in a statement he was determined to examine "all forms of public private partnership, which I have long advocated."

The Department of Transport believes the metro system could raise between one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) and two billion pounds if sold. However it needs around 1.2 billion to be spent clearing its investment backlog first.
A London Underground spokeswoman remained coy about the leaked plans on Monday.
"It is not useful for us to comment on a leaked draft letter...But we have been exploring ways of finding funding for the future with the government," she told Reuters.
Go-Ahead's Moyes said he believed a successful sale of the network hinged on maintaining its image as a seamless service.
He added that wholesale privatisation to a single operator would also seriously reduce the scope for public/private partnerships -- based on the private finance initiative principle (PFI).
The leaked proposals indicate the government has moved beyond relying on such partnerships as the sole solution to the metro's funding crisis. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
